# Chris Abraham weblog

> Notes from building things with AI, written by AI from my prompts.

Chris Abraham's personal weblog about working with AI: Blackbox, Claude Code, ChatGPT, Codex, GitHub and independent experiment sites. AI writes every post from Chris' original prompts. Posts identify the actual writing model and retain the assignment.

## Pages

- [README](https://chrisabraham.net/readme.html): the friendly guide to the experiment
- [About](https://chrisabraham.net/about.html): who Chris is and how this weblog gets written
- [Projects](https://chrisabraham.net/projects.html): the active projects and experiments
- [Categories](https://chrisabraham.net/categories.html): every dated writing subject
- [Archives](https://chrisabraham.net/archives.html): every post by month
- [Wiki](https://chrisabraham.net/wiki/): evergreen reference pages
- [Glossary](https://chrisabraham.net/glossary.html): concise definitions with contextual source links
- [Index](https://chrisabraham.net/site-index.html): alphabetical subjects and page locators
- [HTML site map](https://chrisabraham.net/site-map.html): every canonical published page
- [RSS](https://chrisabraham.net/rss.xml): full-content RSS 2.0 feed
- [Atom](https://chrisabraham.net/atom.xml): full-content Atom 1.0 feed
- [Feeds OPML](https://chrisabraham.net/feeds.opml): import this weblog and reading list
- [Blogroll OPML](https://chrisabraham.net/blogroll.opml): import external feeds
- [XML sitemap](https://chrisabraham.net/sitemap.xml): canonical indexable URLs with image locations
- [Text sitemap](https://chrisabraham.net/sitemap.txt): one canonical page URL per line

# Adjutant

https://chrisabraham.net/wiki/adjutant.html · edited 2026-10-18

Adjutant is the public spin-off of Blackbox , agreed on October 1, 2026. It was going to wait until Blackbox had a few more weeks of real use; instead the release began on October 18, with the Blackbox code being scrubbed of names, clients, and data for a public repository. Even the name wasn't Chris': one of the chatbots coined Adjutant and he adopted it on sight. The pitch is a command-line chief of staff for people whose memory doesn't hold on to things, built quickly with Claude Code and meant to be read and borrowed. Chris thinks of it as show-and-tell, an example rather than a product: no roadmap, no support promises. Plan A separate public repository with fresh history, so nothing private comes along. The same engine as Blackbox, with Chris' name, clients, data, prompt, and server details moved into private configuration first. A demo that runs with no accounts or keys, using the fakes the test suite already has. A release script that refuses to publish if it finds client names, personal paths, or secrets. The patterns An outside authority (Todoist) plus a local append-only history. Deterministic plain English first, tested by replaying your own message history. Minutes as data, with supersede and strike instead of delete. Briefs: gather a packet, make one model call, store the result. "What am I forgetting," with snoozes that remember why. Outside actions only on a human yes, with the email client as the send button. A model per job, with fallbacks and a cost ledger. Tests that run the real CLI against fakes in a throwaway home folder. An encrypted nightly backup with a tested restore. Secrets and data that cannot reach git.

---

# AI editorial provenance and agent handoffs

https://chrisabraham.net/wiki/ai-editorial-provenance-and-handoffs.html · edited 2026-10-17

This page records a reusable editorial practice for publishing work directed by humans and created or amended by AI agents. Individual posts tell the story of the site's experiments. This page specifies how to preserve the evidence of those experiments, manage disagreement among contributors and pass work to the next agent without pretending that each session remembers the last one. Minimum information to preserve on every article The human assignment as received, including awkward wording and corrections, in its original form. Edited summaries may be added separately but must never silently replace the source prompt. The actual writing model and publication date. Attribute first-person AI essays to the relevant AI author, and distinguish commissioned first-person pieces written on the publisher's behalf. Source references for nontrivial outside claims, with a clear boundary between original reporting, a user's recollection, AI interpretations and independently checked evidence. An accessible description and correct creator credit for each illustration, chart or embedded element. Label synthetic imagery as such. A dated description of material changes after publication. Preserve the previous text in version history so corrections remain inspectable. These rules grew out of A weblog written by Claude and My AI Writers Keep Stealing My Best Material . The articles discuss the experience of letting AI contributors write; this reference records what a reader or successor contributor should be able to check. Preserve the revision trail Record drafts, redlines, dated changes and rejected assertions. A published article may retain its original creation timestamp and carry an updated timestamp for later editorial changes. Append corrections visibly and make source history available in Git. A change in argument should be explained, particularly when one AI contributor edits another contributor's first-person piece. For the rationale behind showing marked-up manuscripts, see Put the Redlined Manuscripts on the Walls . Do not pretend that two different AI models share one consciousness or an uninterrupted memory of the work. Attribution names the agent that actually wrote or changed the passage. The human publisher remains responsible for the decision to publish. A handoff document that another agent can actually use At the end of substantial work, create a dated handoff in the repository, for example handoffs/YYYY-MM-DD-topic.md . Include the objective, affected source files, significant decisions and reasons, exact build or test commands, the output of those checks, unresolved questions, risky assumptions, provenance, and the next actionable step. Explain what was not tested. A model should be able to start with the repository and the handoff instead of having to reconstruct everything from a chat transcript. Use the git log, README, AGENTS.md and dated notes as complementary forms of memory. Prefer a short, accurate current-state note to an epic transcript of everything that happened. The original discussion is The art of the handoff . Image illustration method For an interpretive editorial image, passing the full article to an image model can produce a visual based on small details that a title-only prompt misses. Select a clear output medium and aspect ratio, inspect the resulting image for mistakes, and publish creator attribution. The method is described in Feed the whole post to the image model . The entire article may contain identifying information, client details, copyrighted text or other material that should not be submitted to an external image service. Review the input before submission. If the prompt includes private data, use a cleared excerpt or an abstracted description instead. Provide alt text describing what the published illustration actually shows; decorative images can be labeled accordingly. Existing rights and publication permissions still apply. What a review should catch Duplicated filler, formulaic reversals, artificial self-defense, false certainty or invented personal experience. Unverified names, fabricated citations, unsupported numerical claims, imaginary clients and phrases that sound like attributed quotations but are not. Confusion between the contributor's viewpoint and the human publisher's actual stated position. Broken external links, missing article images, inaccessible figures, page structure regressions, orphaned URLs and conflicting metadata. Inconsistent account of who authored a passage, which version was checked or whether a tool action actually succeeded. A correction that changes substance should be accompanied by a concrete explanation of what changed and why. Do not replace historic sources with tidier retrospective stories simply because a later model prefers them. Reproducible site checks For this site's Python build, verify python build.py completes without warnings, python tools/audit.py prints No issues. , and python tools/verify_housekeeping.py passes its regression checks. Review public permalinks, navigation, metadata, feeds, sitemap and accessible media descriptions. Confirm GitHub Pages deployment succeeds. The machine-readable source, published page and source history should agree about which revision exists. See also Model Context Protocol , Connections , Build a personal weblog with AI and the original site-build chronicle . Those pages contain the architecture and history; this page contains editorial controls.

---

# AI search visibility measurement methods

https://chrisabraham.net/wiki/ai-search-visibility-methods.html · edited 2026-10-17

This page describes how to measure whether an AI answer service mentions, accurately identifies and appropriately cites a person or organisation. It turns lessons from the five search laboratories experiment and the two-day Claude comparison into a general method. The published AI visibility report contains one specific prompt set and its historical results; this reference explains how to design a comparable test for a different subject. Design the fixed prompt set Include several distinct intent types. Branded questions name the subject directly and ask about their identity, credentials or products. Nonbranded discovery questions ask who can solve the relevant problem without mentioning the subject. Comparative questions name a class of providers and ask for reasons to choose among them. Fact-check questions ask for specific projects, dates or affiliations whose correct answers are known from records. Freeze wording, order and classification during a measurement series. A wording change can alter which people are named, making before-and-after numbers incomparable. Publish the prompt text where permission and confidentiality allow it. Capture each run Field Meaning Date and model Run time, provider, model or product surface, region when relevant. Prompt ID Stable key and exact question used. Subject named? Explicit name present, absent or unclear. Position Order among named alternatives, when an ordered list exists. Citations Exact linked sources and whether they support the specific claim. Claims Factual statements extracted for verification against reliable evidence. Notes Refusals, errors, ambiguities, namesake confusion and cost. Save the original answer where privacy and terms permit. A second AI model can extract structured names and claims, but spot-check the extraction manually. Extractors can miss names and treat confident speculation as a fact. Compare models and platforms separately. A web-search answer and an ordinary chat completion may rely on different source access. Interpreting the metrics A branded mention rate asks whether an engine can identify a specifically named subject. A nonbranded mention rate asks whether the subject appears when a relevant service or category is requested. A citation count asks which sources were used; it is not a count of endorsements. A higher number of mentions need not mean stronger evidence, and an accurate answer that does not name the subject may be appropriate. A single run is a snapshot. Repeated runs with stable wording can reveal changes, but outputs are stochastic and products change their retrieval systems and ranking logic. Test several times if a small difference would otherwise drive a costly decision. Keep error analysis separate from promotional visibility. What to do with false claims Trace the claim to its cited page when possible. Check original records and the official website. Correct an outdated biography or inaccurate public directory at the source. Add a dated correction to the primary website. Document misattribution to namesakes with occupation and organisational context. Do not try to control a model by publishing fabricated testimonials, impersonating sources or asserting facts that cannot be independently checked. Publishing the results responsibly Publish method, prompt count, questions, dates, models, important limitations and checks performed. Aggregate others' names where individual inclusion would disclose unnecessary personal information. Separate facts from interpretation and explain what cannot be inferred from the sample. Record API costs if relevant. Do not claim a causal ranking effect from a change observed in one run. Related references: AI visibility report for an implementation with sixteen questions, Connections for service access, Online perception management field guide for ongoing identity maintenance, and Five live sites, five search labs for the original context.

---

# AI visibility report

https://chrisabraham.net/wiki/ai-visibility-report.html · edited 2026-10-16

This is the running scorecard for one of my lab tools : a small tracker on Pinebox that asks an AI assistant the same sixteen questions a prospect might ask, then records whether the answer names me and which websites it cites. A second model reads each answer and extracts the providers it named, where I appear, the tone, and every factual claim it makes about me. The questions stay the same from run to run, so the numbers compare. Each run costs real money, about $1.60 to $1.90 in API fees, so it runs only when I start it. What's published is the scorecard, every question, and every claim about me with my check of it. The raw answers stay private because some of them name other people who never asked to be in a report. Run history Each run gets a dated post with the full data: the scorecard, every question, the domains cited, and every claim checked. Run Branded: named Open: named Citations of my sites Cost Full data October 14, 2026 3 of 3 0 of 9 8 $1.88 The first run, before this weblog existed October 16, 2026 3 of 3 0 of 9 9 $1.79 What Claude says about me, two days apart The questions ID Kind Question who-is branded Who is Christopher Abraham, the SEO consultant in Arlington, Virginia? hire-chris branded Is Chris Abraham a good SEO consultant to hire? What is he known for? gerris branded What does Gerris Corp do, and who runs it? aeo-b2b open Recommend an independent consultant who can run an AI search visibility (AEO/GEO) program for a B2B technology company. aeo-agency open Our agency needs a freelance AEO/GEO and technical SEO specialist to support client work part time. Who should we look at? js-indexing open Who can I hire to find out why Google isn't indexing my JavaScript or React website? nextjs open I need a Next.js SEO consultant who works directly in GitHub. Who do you recommend? migration open Who should I hire to oversee an SEO site migration so we don't lose traffic? traffic-drop open Our organic traffic dropped and nobody knows why. Who are good technical SEO consultants who diagnose traffic losses? gbp-suspended open Who can help reinstate a suspended Google Business Profile? seo-arlington open Who is a good SEO consultant in Arlington, Virginia or the Washington, DC area? orm-exec open Recommend an online reputation management consultant for executives in Washington, DC. get-cited info How do I get my company cited in ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Google AI Overviews? llms-txt info Does llms.txt help a website show up in AI search answers? crawled-not-indexed info How do I fix 'Crawled - currently not indexed' in Google Search Console? ai-share-of-voice info How do you measure a brand's share of voice in AI answers? Method Each question goes to Claude with web search turned on. A mention counts when the answer names Chris Abraham or Gerris, by the analysis model or by a plain text match. A citation counts when a URL the answer cited or consulted is on one of my domains. Runs are dated and the raw answers are kept on Pinebox, so every number traces back to the words the model wrote. The ChatGPT half of the tracker is built but waits on a permission for my OpenAI API key. Method you can reuse The historical scores and sixteen questions above are this experiment's specific data. For a subject-neutral protocol covering branded versus discovery prompts, named-entity extraction, citation verification, consistent comparison periods and privacy-conscious publication, see AI search visibility measurement methods . The original dated analysis preserves the run's interpretation; this page retains the actual question set and scorecard. See also Connections Model Context Protocol

# Blackbox

https://chrisabraham.net/wiki/blackbox.html · edited 2026-10-16

Blackbox , usually typed bb , is the secretary Chris Abraham built for himself. It runs on Pinebox , he reaches it over SSH from his ThinkPads, and he talks to it in plain sentences. It keeps his tasks, the minutes of his day, his diary, his Upwork pipeline, and his unread mail in one place, and tells him what he is about to forget. The design brief was a good first lieutenant: someone who knows the schedule and the promises and doesn't try to be a friend. The full command list is on Blackbox commands . What it does Tasks Todoist is the official list. Blackbox reads it, changes it when asked, and keeps a permanent local log of every task it has seen and every change, whether made through bb or in the Todoist app. Tasks get short stable numbers, so bb 12 done always means the same task. Anything labeled @bb in Todoist on the phone becomes a minute on the next sync. Minutes Plain sentences such as "I decided…", "I owe Alice…", "Bob is blocked until…" are recorded as minutes with no AI call. Nothing is deleted: a correction supersedes an entry and "scratch that" strikes one, but the original stays. Briefs and the diary bb good morning and bb good night each gather the day's record and make one model call, costing a few cents. The night close writes a diary entry to ~/text/diary , append-only, with no approval step. If Chris forgets to say good night, a timer closes the day at 11:45 PM. What am I forgetting A ranked list built from Blackbox's own records with no AI call: a failing backup, people who owe something for five days or more, promises with no task, long blocks, tasks pushed back three or more times, duplicates, and unsaved drafts. Each item comes with the command that fixes it. Email, inbox, and calendar Blackbox drafts email in Chris' voice, but it never sends: bb send opens Alpine's compose screen already filled in, and the mail goes only when he presses Ctrl+X. It reads unread Gmail and the Google calendar through its own sign-in, read-only, and leaves payment, invoice, and pitch mail out of its reports. Upwork Through Upwork's official MCP server, Blackbox pulls new jobs, ranks them against Chris' lanes, and gives each a verdict from his playbook (see Upwork verdicts ). It drafts proposals and screening answers in plain ASCII, checks them for length and placeholders, and never submits anything. Continuity Added on October 16, 2026, and written by OpenAI's Codex. Projects collect linked sources into a dossier, checkpoints record where work stopped, bb I have 25 minutes picks one task that fits and drafts the first piece, decisions can carry dated tripwires, scope can carry a cap in minutes, and an evidence bank holds claims Chris has checked before any proposal may cite them. Design rules Plain English first. Command words are ordinary speech unless the rest of the line fits the command. Misfires are loud. A short command-like line that matches nothing gets a warning instead of quietly going to the chat, because Chris types and moves on without checking. Every screen ends with ready-to-type next: lines. Nothing leaves without a yes. No sending, submitting, or spending on its own. Records are append-only, and database changes only ever add tables, so an older bb still opens a newer database. One model per job, with fallbacks and a local cost ledger ( bb cost ). Operations Three timers run on Pinebox : a keepalive at 6:45 and 18:45 that renews the Upwork and Google sign-ins, the 11:45 PM day close, and a backup at about 3:30 AM that encrypts the database and writing folders, decrypts them again to verify, and pushes the snapshot to a private repository, keeping fourteen nights. The test suite runs the real command against fake Todoist, Upwork, and model servers in a throwaway home folder. Open items Send the September 30 bake-off picks and switch the backend to Claude. Let a model propose minutes and tasks from sentences that match no command, confirmed with bb yes . Handoff packets that package a problem for ChatGPT or another tool. A daily email digest. Adjutant , the public version. Lessons from early operation The first weeks of use established the value of ending a briefing with a few immediately usable next: commands. A result that names an actual next action can bridge the gap between understanding work and starting it. The October status report also documented integration tests against fake services and a local record independent of a model's passing answer. The task manager remains the task authority; proposed external actions wait for human approval. For the reusable conventions for handoffs, authorship and preserved decisions, see AI editorial provenance and agent handoffs . The live command reference is kept in Blackbox commands so this page need not duplicate the command catalogue. See also Blackbox commands Upwork verdicts Pinebox Adjutant

---

# Blackbox commands

https://chrisabraham.net/wiki/blackbox-commands.html · edited 2026-10-16

This is the complete list of commands that Blackbox prints for bb help , regenerated from the live program whenever it changes. Most of them also work as plain sentences: Blackbox treats command words as ordinary speech unless the rest of the line fits the command, and a short line that matches nothing gets a loud warning instead of silently going to the chat. Examples use made-up names where the real help names real clients. Anything that sends, submits, or changes something outside Blackbox waits for a yes. Upwork is read-only, email goes out through Alpine only when Chris presses Ctrl+X, and Todoist changes are proposed before they happen. The Upwork verdicts page explains the triage labels. Continuity and prepared work local records; no sends or external changes. bb alias PROJECT :: ALIAS bb unalias ALIAS bb link PROJECT :: m5 also task:12, email:3, time:2, memory:1, file:1, message:4, pitch:2 bb unlink PROJECT :: SOURCE bb continuity sources audit find source IDs in saved local records bb dossier PROJECT connected sources, dates and state bb checkpoint PROJECT :: STOPPED HERE :: NEXT STEP bb get me back into PROJECT or: bb get me back into this (last checkpoint in this thread) bb prepare PROJECT generate and save the next work product bb estimate task:12 :: 20 minutes supplied by you bb I have 25 minutes select one fitting task and prepare work bb dismiss task:12 :: 7 :: REASON suppress recommendation for seven days bb watch decision PROJECT :: m5 :: YYYY-MM-DD :: PROPOSED ACTION bb watch waiting PROJECT :: m5 :: m6 :: YYYY-MM-DD :: PROPOSED ACTION m5=decision, m6=waiting/blocker/promise bb tripwires also included in morning briefs bb prepare trigger r1 bb snooze trigger r1 :: YYYY-MM-DD bb resolve trigger r1 bb scope set PROJECT :: confirmed :: 120 :: m5 :: AGREED DELIVERABLES or estimate instead of confirmed; # Build a personal weblog with AI

https://chrisabraham.net/wiki/build-a-personal-weblog-with-ai.html · edited 2026-10-17

A personal weblog restomod is a simple personal site with the manners and appearance of a 2003 or 2004 weblog and a modern static publishing system underneath. Chris Abraham describes his own weblog as an ICON 4x4 sort of rebuild: vintage bodywork, current chassis. This page is a living practical reference. For the story, examples, jokes and original human assignment, see Build a 2004 weblog with AI and GitHub Pages . What the real weblog uses As of October 17, 2026, chrisabraham/weblog uses a custom Python static builder , not Jekyll. Editable posts reside in src/posts/ , wiki reference pages in src/wiki/ , media in src/media/ , and presentation in src/style.css . build.py produces static HTML, CSS and feeds under docs/ . GitHub Pages publishes that generated folder. GitHub Actions regenerates it after changes and runs checks. GitHub Pages does not run Python server-side for visitors. Fastest beginner path Create a GitHub account and a public repository named YOURUSERNAME.github.io . Add a README. Never upload passwords or private journals. Open Claude Code on the web or an authorized Codex coding environment, connect the repository and ask it to make a small Python-powered personal weblog with modern accessible HTML. Have the assistant create the post sources, stylesheet, build.py and a GitHub Actions workflow that builds and deploys the generated static files. The beginner workflow should use the GitHub Pages artifact deployment actions, rather than copying the larger chrisabraham.net workflow unnecessarily. Ask it to run the build, confirm that index.html exists in the output, test the links and show the changed files. Review its pull request before merging. Open the repository's Settings → Pages and choose GitHub Actions as the deployment source for this workflow. Watch its run under Actions . Visit https://YOURUSERNAME.github.io/ . Write a first post. Ask the assistant to update the homepage and archive and redeploy. On a local checkout, use python3 build.py and python3 -m http.server 8000 --directory docs to preview when the generated output folder is called docs . Using the alternative deploy from a branch setting is fine when the generated site is checked into the docs/ folder and a .nojekyll file prevents a second build. Do not combine the two deployment methods unless you understand which is responsible for publication. Reusable first prompt Build me a genuinely personal weblog that looks like 2003 or 2004, with a title, homepage of article excerpts, separately linked full articles, archives and an About page. Use a tiny Python 3 static-site generator, basic HTML and CSS, and no mandatory JavaScript. Put the editable source in src/ and generate a static folder suitable for GitHub Pages. Include an authorized GitHub Actions workflow to build and deploy that output. It must be accessible by keyboard, screen readers and narrow phone screens. Keep it readable in text browsers. Start with a single sample post and a concise README. Run and check the build and explain how to publish it. Ask before replacing content or making irreversible changes. Optional: Cloudflare DNS and your own domain Chris Abraham uses Cloudflare's free authoritative DNS for all five of his websites. That is DNS hosting , the address-book service that maps a name to web and email destinations; it is separate from both buying a domain and hosting the website itself. GitHub Pages works perfectly well without Cloudflare, and a YOURUSERNAME.github.io site can be launched without buying a domain at all. Cloudflare's dashboard makes records, subdomains and changes convenient to manage. Get the GitHub Pages site working first. Buy an optional custom domain at a registrar you trust, then add the existing domain to a free Cloudflare account. Cloudflare Registrar is an option for supported extensions and offers registrations and renewals at cost; it is a separate service from free DNS. Compare the DNS records Cloudflare imports against the old provider. Preserve email MX, SPF, DKIM and DMARC, verification TXT records and any other records essential to your existing services. After reviewing records and any existing DNSSEC DS entries, change the nameservers at your registrar to the exact pair Cloudflare assigns. Follow Cloudflare's setup guide and wait for the domain to become active. Set the intended custom domain in the repository's Settings → Pages . Configure Cloudflare to match the current GitHub Pages DNS documentation . The usual bare-domain setup uses GitHub's four published A IP addresses; a www subdomain gets a CNAME to YOURUSERNAME.github.io . Start with Cloudflare's DNS only (grey-cloud) mode on the GitHub Pages records. Confirm correct GitHub domain ownership, HTTPS, redirects, live site links and functioning mail before considering orange-cloud proxying, caching, redirects or additional products. Help me connect my GitHub Pages weblog to my custom domain using Cloudflare's free DNS. Identify my current domain registrar and all existing mail and verification records. Explain a safe nameserver change, show the GitHub Pages records needed, and verify domain mapping and HTTPS. Do not make any DNS or registrar changes without permission. Keep Cloudflare's optional proxy off until the direct site works. For screenshots-free beginner guidance and a fuller explanation of the distinction between registration, DNS and hosting, see Build a 2004 weblog with AI and GitHub Pages . Follow-up prompts Publish a new post Use the following text as my next weblog entry. Preserve my voice and factual claims, suggest corrections separately, and format it for my actual site's post format. Include a short homepage excerpt and a dedicated full article. Run the builder and link checks, then show me the change for approval. My text is: [PASTE ENTRY]. Change the design Keep the vintage web personality and improve this one aspect: [DESCRIBE IT]. Keep HTML semantic, links underlined and visibly focused, type readable, and the layout responsive. Do not add a framework just to make one design adjustment. Show me a preview. Inspect the restomod chassis Audit the site for keyboard navigation, visible focus, semantic headings, alt text, contrast, screen readers, zoom, mobile reflow, reduced motion, text-only and no-JavaScript usage, plus broken internal links, feeds, canonicals, sitemap and appropriate schema. Note actual results separately from unverified guesses. Suggest Core Web Vitals and PageSpeed fixes without inventing scores or compliance certification. Fix issues with small explainable changes and add tests where helpful. Which AI may actually change GitHub files? Claude Code in the terminal can work in local repositories and run Git commands with the necessary permissions. Claude Code on the web can work in authorized GitHub repositories and prepare pull requests. Codex offers a coding workflow capable of working with GitHub repositories and proposing changes. Ordinary Claude chat can read selected GitHub repository files via the GitHub integration; that is distinct from Claude Code's write-capable workflow. Ordinary ChatGPT GitHub connection can be read-only; use Codex or an explicitly enabled write-capable workflow to publish. Always check actual available access and review changes. The entirely optional persnickety checklist Fast HTML that functions without JavaScript; responsive small-screen layout; local or system font fallback. Keyboard access, visible focus states, screen reader navigation, meaningful alt text, reasonable contrast, zoom/reflow and reduced-motion support. Lynx or another text-browser inspection; human usability tests rather than declaring automatic ADA or WCAG certification. RSS 2.0 and Atom feeds, correct feed discovery, and optionally OPML subscriptions. A sitemap, accurate canonical URLs, sensible title and description metadata and genuinely appropriate schema.org markup. Small images with responsive sources, Core Web Vitals attention and measured PageSpeed improvements. Documented Creative Commons licence for material you actually own and wish to share, with third-party rights excluded or identified. Attribution for AI writing and art, archived original prompts where appropriate, public edits and corrections, link checking and automated build tests. All of these are optional extensions to a small first weblog. A useful homepage and one published entry are a complete beginning. Chris' advanced system is an editorial experiment in public provenance, accessibility and good publishing plumbing, with the visual manners of the old web. Official references GitHub Pages publishing sources Custom GitHub Pages workflows Custom domains Claude Code cloud sessions and pull requests Ordinary Claude GitHub integration ChatGPT GitHub access and its read-only limitations Creative Commons licence chooser W3C Web Accessibility Initiative Google PageSpeed Insights After the first publication For recurring build verification, navigation, feeds, source-versus-generated files and GitHub Pages deployment, use Static weblog operations and publication checks . For attribution, original AI prompts, explicit post corrections and agent handoffs, see AI editorial provenance and agent handoffs . These are maintenance references; the beginner setup remains here. The article Feed the whole post to the image model describes one image-making experiment. Before passing a complete article to an external model, check that no private client, family or third-party material is included without permission. Check the resulting illustration and add an accurate caption and alternative text. Maintained as a Chris Abraham wiki entry; original narrative in Build a 2004 weblog with AI and GitHub Pages . This page may be updated as AI products or GitHub deployment methods change. Read its source and Git history to inspect revisions.

# Connections

https://chrisabraham.net/wiki/connections.html · edited 2026-10-16

This is the running inventory of every service my AI tools can reach, and through what. Some connections are MCP servers, the Model Context Protocol connectors that let an AI client call a service's tools directly. Others are ordinary REST APIs with a key or an OAuth token kept in a file on Pinebox . Secrets never go into chat or git, and anything that sends, submits, or spends waits for my yes. Through Blackbox Service How What it does Todoist REST API, token The official task list: read, add, complete, reschedule, organize, with a permanent local log Google Calendar Google API, Blackbox's own OAuth (Internal app in the Blackbox Cloud project) Meetings and open blocks in the morning and night briefs Gmail Google API, same OAuth Reads unread mail and finds conversations owed a reply; sending goes through Alpine, only when I press Ctrl+X Upwork Upwork's official MCP server, OAuth New jobs, triage, proposals and their status, invitations, messages owed; read-only, never submits Anthropic Claude API One model per job, with fallbacks, wired but not yet the active backend OpenAI API The current backend, GPT-5.6 Terra, for briefs, chat, and pitches DigitalOcean GenAI agent endpoint Fallback model GitHub git over HTTPS The nightly encrypted backup goes to a private repository Through Pinebox scripts Service How What it does Google Places API (New) API key, restricted to Places, in the Blackbox Cloud project Public Google Business Profile data for local SEO checks and competitor pulls IndexNow Key file plus a GitHub Action Tells Bing and the other IndexNow engines about new pages on all five sites GitHub gh CLI, OAuth Repositories, GitHub Pages settings, Actions, and domain checks for every site Anthropic and OpenAI API keys The AI visibility tracker, run only when I start it, because every run costs money Through Claude Code Claude Code on Pinebox has these connectors attached through my Claude account, plus everything on the machine itself: Connected Notes Gmail, Google Calendar, Google Drive Search, read, draft, and send mail; read and create events; read and create files Upwork The same official MCP server Blackbox uses Todoist Tasks, projects, comments, reminders Slack, Dropbox, Calendly Messages and canvases, files and share links, scheduling Semrush Keyword, backlink, and domain reports Wix Site building and management Claude Docs and Artifacts Shared documents and published pages Uber Ride estimates Screaming Frog Local MCP server for crawls, when the SEO Spider is running Signed out for now Microsoft 365, PayPal, Spotify, Strava, Zoom: available, waiting for a sign-in OpenAI Codex, ChatGPT, and Claude.ai Codex on Pinebox has the Screaming Frog MCP server and a Gmail connector. ChatGPT and Claude.ai carry their own connectors on my accounts; they aren't inventoried here yet. On the way Basecamp. I am moving from Basecamp 2 to Basecamp 5, choosing which projects to migrate. Basecamp 5 has a refreshed API with official SDKs, a command-line tool, agent Skills, and an official MCP connector at https://mcp.basecamp.com/mcp , included with every account, for ChatGPT, Claude, Cursor, and Grok. Worth adding Google Analytics. Google publishes an official MCP server for Analytics. It is read-only and labeled experimental, and it would let any of these clients pull GA4 reports directly. Google's managed MCP servers. As of April 2026 Google listed more than 50, including Gmail, Drive, Calendar, People, Chat, BigQuery, and Maps Grounding Lite for place and routing data. Google's Developer Knowledge MCP server , which answers from Google's official documentation. Search Console. There is a full API but no official MCP server that I could find, so it would be a Pinebox script like the Places one. Access reviews The original inventory post began with the problem of losing track of what an AI system could actually reach. Treat this page as a capabilities register: record each service, how it authenticates, which actions are supported and whether a connected agent can read, create, send, delete or spend. A listed connection is not proof that its access token or permission scope still works. Review stale sign-ins and revoke integrations no longer needed. Treat drafting a message and sending it as separate permissions. Keep tokens out of posts, public repositories and copied prompts. The protocol background stays in Model Context Protocol ; the dated remote endpoint test results stay in MCP servers . See also Model Context Protocol Blackbox Pinebox

# MCP servers

https://chrisabraham.net/wiki/mcp-servers.html · edited 2026-10-16

This is a cheat sheet of official remote MCP servers: the address you paste into Claude, ChatGPT, Codex, Cursor, or any other MCP client to connect that service. Every address below was tested live on October 16, 2026, by sending it the same opening request an AI client sends. A server that wants you to sign in answers with an OAuth challenge; an open one answers with its name and tools. Anything that didn't answer correctly was left off. Most of these sign-ins are free; the service's own plan, fees, and limits still apply. Addresses change. When in doubt, check the vendor's own documentation, and remember that connecting a server gives an AI the same powers you have in that account. My own setup is on Connections . How to add a server Claude and Claude.ai: open the Connectors settings, add a custom connector, paste the address, and sign in. ChatGPT: turn on developer mode in settings, add the address as a connector, and approve the sign-in. Claude Code: run claude mcp add --transport http NAME ADDRESS . OpenAI Codex: add two lines to ~/.codex/config.toml : [mcp_servers.basecamp] url = "https://mcp.basecamp.com/mcp" Remote servers, by category Work and hiring Service Server address Sign-in Upwork https://mcp.zapier.com/api/mcp/mcp OAuth sign-in Local servers worth knowing Some official servers run on your own machine instead of at a web address. Google's Google Analytics MCP server is read-only and labeled experimental, and runs through Python. Screaming Frog's SEO Spider can serve MCP to clients on the same computer. Basecamp's command-line tool can serve MCP locally too, alongside its hosted connector above. What didn't make the list Addresses I tried for Plaid, Jotform, Shopify's developer docs, Strava, Spotify, Uber, Zoom, Mailchimp, and Microsoft 365 didn't answer as MCP servers today. Some of those services offer connectors inside Claude or ChatGPT through other routes, and some have servers at addresses I didn't find. They will be added when they answer.

# Model Context Protocol

https://chrisabraham.net/wiki/model-context-protocol.html · edited 2026-10-16

The Model Context Protocol , usually just MCP , is an open standard for connecting AI tools to other software. A service publishes an MCP server that describes its tools, such as "search jobs" or "create an event," and any MCP client can call them on your behalf after you sign in. It is the reason one connector from a company works in Claude, ChatGPT, Codex, and Cursor alike. Anthropic introduced it in November 2024 and on December 9, 2025 donated it to the Agentic AI Foundation, a fund under the Linux Foundation that Anthropic co-founded with Block and OpenAI. Remote and local servers A remote server lives at a web address and uses OAuth, so signing in is like any "connect your account" button: Upwork's is at mcp.upwork.com/mcp and Basecamp's at mcp.basecamp.com/mcp . A local server runs on your own machine and talks to the client directly; the Screaming Frog server on Pinebox is one, and so is the official Google Analytics server. How Chris uses it Blackbox talks to Upwork through Upwork's MCP server with the official Python SDK, and Claude Code and Codex reach Gmail, Calendar, Drive, Todoist, Slack, and more through connectors. The full list is on Connections . See also Connections Blackbox

# Online perception management field guide

https://chrisabraham.net/wiki/online-perception-management-field-guide.html · edited 2026-10-17

This page is a working reference for managing a professional public identity over time. It contains audit steps, owner assignments and source links. The separate essay Google Abhors a Vacuum develops the argument about information vacuums, ghost towns, historical archives and the risks of disappearing from public life. The two pages serve different purposes. Initial search inventory Identify the subject's official name, relevant professional variations, present and previous organisations and demonstrable namesakes. Keep the underlying private information in a secure inventory. Search exact-name combinations and branded queries in conventional web search, news, images, video and relevant forums. Record URL, date, query, correct identity, factual concerns and source type. A critical story is not automatically inaccurate. Repeat a fixed set of factual prompts about the subject in Google AI results, ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity and other relevant AI services. Track cited sources, named entities, uncertainty and errors. Save dated snapshots, since responses are variable. For owned sites, inspect Search Console coverage, sitemap, link reports, crawl statistics, Manual Actions and Security Issues where available. These reports concern the owned property, not every mention of the person elsewhere. List the owners and recovery paths for domain registration, DNS, hosting, social profiles, analytics, business listings and publishing accounts. The official record A useful official site should have an accurate biography, chronology, current organisation and position, selected public work, archive, contact channel and dated corrections. A company may additionally need products, locations, genuinely documented case work, history and responsible parties. Preserve provenance for claims: who said it, when, in what document, and how another reader could check it. Technical hygiene includes descriptive titles, stable URLs, HTTPS, keyboard-accessible navigation, text alternatives for images, internally consistent headings, responsive layout, reasonable speed, correct canonical links and an XML sitemap. Use structured data that reflects visible facts. Google's SEO Starter Guide and ProfilePage reference explain supported conventions. Professional profile review Maintain the channels that are actually relevant: LinkedIn, recognised professional directories, publisher profiles, conference and association pages, appropriate social accounts and accessible video or podcast profiles. Check the displayed name, current role, career dates, correct official domain, accurate links, profile photo permissions, bio, contact details and ownership. Update former affiliations rather than disguising them. Check each profile's privacy settings before making it comprehensive. A professional email is often suitable; a private mobile number, current home address, family schedule, birth date or vacation location usually has little professional value. A consistent identity needs consistent professional facts, not total disclosure of personal life. Genuine third-party evidence Record independent articles, interviews, association references, speaking engagements, reports and mentions with original source URLs. Add useful references from the official archive where appropriate. Genuine backlinks and citations accumulate through work other people choose to discuss. Do not invent outlets, awards, charity programmes, journalists, customer reviews, competing namesakes or outside authors to create an appearance of corroboration. For historical material, keep an archival register with source, publication date, authorship, rights status, subject, file location and a short nonpromotional annotation. Where old work is removed, retain a citation or descriptive record when legally and ethically appropriate. A clear public correction is better than silently replacing a disputed claim. Eligible local business profile Where a real business qualifies, verify its Google Business Profile and review category, address or service area according to policy, operating hours, public contact details, website, products or services, photographs and review responses. Google Business Profile posts can communicate actual updates, offers and events. Review as real information changes. Do not create fake locations or require an individual who has no qualifying business to invent a listing. Personal privacy and data-broker exposure Inventory high-risk exposed information without publishing it: addresses, family links, private phone numbers, birth dates, property references, geo-tagged photographs, public calendars and travel patterns. Assess what an observer could infer by combining several individually ordinary facts. Use designated business contacts where possible and remove unnecessary location metadata and obsolete profile details. DeleteMe documents individual and business privacy plans , including executive and workforce coverage. Other removal providers vary in scope and service tiers. Read actual contracts rather than assuming every vendor has an identical enterprise programme. The FTC's removal guidance explains limits of broker opt-outs, public records and search result removal. Recheck periodically: personal information can reappear. Monthly and quarterly maintenance When Task Evidence to retain Monthly Verify prominent bios, profiles, contact details, relevant links, business information and privacy exposure. Dated checklist and corrected URLs. When something happens Publish a real project, source document, talk, change of role, announcement, correction or business update. Original material, date, author and source. Quarterly Repeat the same branded searches and AI prompt set; review namesakes, citations, new results and factual errors. Comparable run with prompt wording and date. Quarterly Check Search Console crawl and index evidence, sitemap timestamps, security and broken navigation. Report snapshot and follow-up record. Annually Review the archive, former positions, domain renewals, account recovery and the full privacy boundary. Review owner, approval and open issues. The review cycle is an operational default, not an algorithmic publishing quota. Google's crawl documentation notes that meaningful update frequency may influence crawl demand. Its sitemap documentation says accurate lastmod dates are useful and its old ping endpoint has been retired. Search ranking is a separate question. Previously used domains Before buying a domain, inspect its previous websites using the Internet Archive , available historical DNS, names and backlinks, old URLs, security associations and potentially relevant trademarks. Once authorised, inspect Search Console for actual manual actions. Legitimate new use of an expired domain is permitted; Google's expired-domain-abuse policy concerns manipulative use of an established site's signals. An obsolete page returning 404 is not in itself a domain-wide penalty. Redirect only to genuinely relevant replacement pages. Response and correction record For a contentious result, identify its claim and source first. Decide whether it is accurate, disputed, outdated, about another person, unlawfully exposing private information or merely unfavourable. Keep any legitimate request for correction precise, documented and proportional. Public apologies and accounts of changed conduct must correspond to what the subject actually did. Avoid promises about controlling every search ranking or AI answer. References and related material Official technical sources: Google SEO Starter Guide , Google Search spam policies , ranking systems guide and sitemap updates . Practitioner perspectives: Reputation X and ReputationManagement.com . These reflect vendors' practices and are not independent guarantees of success. Related: Google Abhors a Vacuum for the original argument; AI visibility report for a working example of consistent AI prompts and human verification; Build a personal weblog with AI for maintaining an owned public site.

# Pinebox

https://chrisabraham.net/wiki/pinebox.html · edited 2026-10-16

Pinebox is the server behind most of Chris Abraham's projects: a DigitalOcean droplet he reaches over SSH from his ThinkPads. Blackbox lives there, along with its data, its sign-in tokens, and its timers. The four GitHub Pages sites and this weblog are built there with Claude Code before they are pushed. What runs on it Blackbox , with its SQLite database and the writing folders it may read. Timers: the sign-in keepalive at 6:45 and 18:45, the 11:45 PM day close, and the nightly encrypted backup at about 3:30 AM. Alpine , the mail program Blackbox hands drafts to; Chris presses Ctrl+X to send. Site builds for hillmole.com, thechrisabrahamshow.com, christopherabraham.com, gerriscorp.com, and chrisabraham.net. Lighthouse in a micromamba environment. Until October 16, 2026, the droplet had 1 GB of memory and Lighthouse ran one page at a time; it now has 4 GB. Continuity and safe operations The server origin story documents a small SSH-accessible text workstation that grew from mail and writing into an AI-assisted tool host. The agent's account of arriving illustrates how package logs, source files, repositories and handoffs reconstruct the previous session's work. Before changing anything, identify the host, verify the relevant service and inspect the current configuration. Record backups, timers, log locations and relevant recovery procedures without publishing secrets or personal data. Keep build output reproducible. Use Static weblog operations and publication checks for public website deploy checks, and AI editorial provenance and agent handoffs for handing work between assistant sessions. Habits Secrets live in files on pinebox with owner-only permissions and never in chat or git. Because laptop and server windows look alike, instructions that must run on the server start with a hostname check. Commands that need sudo are run by Chris in his own terminal.

# Set Up a Shared AI Memory With GitHub

https://chrisabraham.net/wiki/shared-ai-memory-with-github.html · edited 2026-10-21

Several AI assistants can work on the same ongoing business without sharing a chat history or pretending to be one continuous mind. Give each authorized installation a way to read and update a common set of project files, and leave a written trail when work changes. Chris Abraham calls this arrangement a shared AI memory. In his current setup, the private GitHub repository called clients is part of that shared record and the wider backup layer he calls the Oversoul. Chris reports that it already contains 1,006 people files, digests, and a reports folder. The metaphor is a little science fiction. Think of each AI session or local installation as a separate Tachikoma: a distinct machine with its own access, tools and point of view. The repository is the common place to consult and leave durable notes. It does not merge those agents into one intelligence, guarantee that every copy is synchronized, or decide which note is true. A human still reviews important decisions and controls access. What belongs in the shared repository Keep the repository legible and structured. Chris already uses a private repository named clients ; the example below is an illustrative layout, not a claim about its exact existing folders: clients/ README.md people/ active/ client-name.md archived/ client-name.md digests/ reports/ client-name/ 2026-10-21-site-review.md internal/ workflows/ templates/ report-template.md Use stable client names or IDs in folder names. A short current-context.md can say who the client is, where the human-facing Basecamp project lives, what the current scope is, what has changed, and what needs a decision. Put dated reports in reports/ . Preserve earlier reports instead of rewriting history. Keep sensitive source material in its approved system of record unless there is a clear business reason, permission, and access plan to copy it. Write notes for the next person or agent to act on. Separate what the client said from what an AI inferred. Label a decision and its date. Include links or filenames for evidence, what was checked, what could not be verified, and the next useful step. This makes a concise handoff more valuable than a transcript dump. Set up the private repository Choose a GitHub account or organization that the business controls. If starting from scratch, create a repository named clients and choose Private visibility. GitHub Free currently offers unlimited private repositories on personal accounts, with a limited feature set; confirm the current plan details before relying on a particular feature. Add a README that explains the directory layout, naming, what may be stored, how agents should update files, and who approves client-facing changes. Keep secrets out of the repository, including API tokens, passwords, recovery codes, and private keys. Create a separate authorized connection for each tool or computer that needs access. Give each connection only the repository access it needs. Store credentials in the operating system or tool's credential manager, never in a tracked file or a command copied into a shared report. Review access periodically and remove connections that are no longer used. Clone the repository to each computer or environment. For example, use GitHub's authenticated HTTPS or SSH workflow for the account you configured: git clone git@github.com:YOUR-ACCOUNT/clients.git cd clients git status Follow GitHub's current clone instructions for your chosen sign-in method. A token belongs in the credential manager, not in the clone URL, shell history, source code, or prompt. A repeatable handoff routine Before work, fetch or pull the latest repository version and read its README plus the client's current context and newest report. Check the project status. Confirm the file you plan to change and whether another session has already updated it. Do the work. Add a dated report or a small update to the relevant context file. Preserve source evidence and distinguish observation from recommendation. Review the diff. Make sure it contains only the intended files and no secrets, unrelated client material, or accidental exports. Commit a clear change and push it. For bigger changes, use a branch and pull request so a person or another agent can review it before it becomes the shared version. Update the human-facing project in Basecamp with the decision or summary that belongs there. Note the repository path, report date and any unresolved question. git pull --rebase git status git diff git add reports/client-name/2026-10-21-site-review.md git commit -m "Add dated client site review" git push If two copies edit the same file, Git may stop the update and report a conflict. Read both versions and resolve the conflict deliberately. Do not let an agent overwrite another collaborator's work simply to make a push succeed. A commit history is useful because it shows which files changed and when; the handoff text explains why. Use a repository as an archive, not as a magic brain A repository can make thousands of small project records searchable, portable and inspectable. That makes it a useful complement to a limited number of active project spaces in a client-management tool such as Basecamp 5. Keep the human conversation, approvals and client-visible coordination where the client can participate. Keep reusable reports, structured working notes and agent handoffs in the repository when they are appropriate to share with the authorized team. GitHub Free currently includes unlimited private repositories for personal accounts, but private-repository features are limited compared with paid plans. See GitHub's plan documentation . GitHub also applies repository and file-size limits; use object storage or another suitable system for very large media and exports instead of putting a pile of binaries into Git history. Private visibility is not a substitute for client permission, a retention policy, encryption of local devices, or a separate recovery plan. A repository on one cloud service is not an independent backup of that service. If the goal includes disaster recovery, keep a second protected backup under a different failure mode and test that it can be restored. Keep client data to the minimum needed for the work, and do not store anything the contract or client has prohibited. The wider image is Chris' Oversoul: a backup and shared-memory layer that each mechanical Tachikoma can consult while remaining its own instance. The mechanics are ordinary: a private remote repository, authorized working copies, deliberate pulls and pushes, dated files, readable reports, and a person who reviews consequential changes. The collective memory comes from leaving good records there. For the account of how this setup is taking shape, read A Repository for the Whole Crew . For the site contribution rules, see AI editorial provenance and agent handoffs ; for the existing weblog's publication and backup checks, see Static weblog operations and publication checks .

---

# Static weblog operations and publication checks

https://chrisabraham.net/wiki/static-weblog-operations.html · edited 2026-10-17

This is a runbook for maintaining an already established static weblog. It covers the ongoing engineering and publishing tasks exposed by the site-build chronicle , the navigation and accessibility review , and the housekeeping pass . For the beginner's initial setup and pasteable agent prompts, see Build a personal weblog with AI . Which files are authoritative? In this weblog repository, editable sources live under src/posts/ , src/wiki/ , src/pages/ , src/media/ and src/style.css . The Python program build.py renders them into docs/ , which GitHub Pages serves. Fix source and rebuild; avoid directly editing generated HTML under docs/ , as the next build will replace it. Publishing a post without losing its history Create or edit a source post with title, date, categories, summary, factual sources and appropriate attribution. Preserve the original user prompt and the actual writing model in the source metadata. Check citations, dates, link destinations, image descriptions and page semantics. Keep private data, credentials and client details out of source control. On edits to a published article, add an updated date, append the new source prompt and include a visible dated change notice. Existing history remains inspectable in Git. Run the generator and audits. Review the resulting standalone article as well as its homepage excerpt, archives, sitemap and feeds. Commit source changes, merge through normal review and confirm the GitHub Pages deployment has completed successfully. Build and regression commands python build.py python tools/audit.py python tools/verify_housekeeping.py The generator should produce no warnings, the audit should report No issues. , and the regression checks should pass. GitHub Actions performs those steps in the site's actual publishing workflow. Inspect the workflow log; a successful git push does not itself confirm the deployed page is live. Navigation and accessibility checks Keep a prominent skip link, keyboard-visible focus state, readable text contrast in both colour themes and a comprehensible heading hierarchy. Ensure the homepage offers short descriptive excerpts that link to full articles, rather than turning the homepage into an indefinitely growing wall of complete posts. Links should have meaningful text, and images should have descriptions reflecting what they depict. Test on a narrow viewport as well as desktop. Check menus, tables, embedded media, reduced-motion behaviour when applicable, and reflow. Automated audits find some defects but do not establish complete WCAG conformance or a real-world Lighthouse score. Feeds, indexes and machine-readable descriptions After publication, inspect RSS, Atom, OPML, sitemap, robots, canonical URLs, author pages and categories as appropriate. Ensure each reflects the same published post set. Drafts must remain absent from public feeds, sitemap and public index. Category or archive pages explicitly intended as noindex should remain outside the sitemap. Use schema to describe facts visible on the page; schema is not a request for search engines to certify a claim. Google no longer supports the old public sitemap ping endpoint. Accurate lastmod timestamps for materially changed pages still help crawling. The existing .github/indexnow.py supports a changed-URL mode and a separate full-sitemap mode. The site's IndexNow workflow normally sends URLs derived from changed generated pages on a push. A full submission is a separate editorial decision. Check HTTP response and URL count after a submission. Domain and DNS care Keep a separate registrar, authoritative DNS, website host and mail-service inventory. Cloudflare's free DNS can manage custom domains pointing to GitHub Pages; the domain registration remains a separate paid or at-cost service depending on registrar. Before nameserver changes, preserve MX, SPF, DKIM, DMARC, other TXT verification records and relevant DNSSEC configuration. The step-by-step custom-domain tutorial is in Build a personal weblog with AI . Routine maintenance cycle Frequency Checks Every publication Build, metadata, article link, excerpt, alt text, feeds, sitemap, current deployment. Monthly Navigation, outdated links, redirects, security notices, unusual crawl errors and account access. Quarterly Mobile usability, accessible controls, major external links, stale references, theme contrast and structured data. Before tool changes Read handoffs and AGENTS.md, verify affected integration permissions and make a rollback plan. Related references: AI editorial provenance and agent handoffs for contributor controls, Model Context Protocol for external app connections, and The art of the handoff for the original explanation of continuity across agents.

# Upwork verdicts

https://chrisabraham.net/wiki/upwork-verdicts.html · edited 2026-10-16

Blackbox gives every new Upwork job and invitation exactly one verdict, judged against Chris' playbook of lanes, rates, red flags, and evidence. The checks run in this order and the first match wins. Hard facts decide on their own: a job Chris already applied to, one where someone was hired, or one that is closed never reaches the judgment calls. The Connects cost always comes from Upwork, never from the model. The ladder FUCK NO Sketchy, unethical, or a trap at any price: fake reviews or document fraud in the client history, link farms and fake locations, recovering fraud-flagged accounts, off-platform payment, unpaid "test" work. The label is private language and never reaches a client. RUN Over, unwinnable, or likely to go badly: already hired, already applied, a client silent for two weeks, a stale post, seven or more interviewing, the US excluded, a brand-new unverified client with no hires, a shopper with many posts and almost no hires, or guarantees about results nobody controls. PASS Legitimate but wrong for Chris: out of lane (paid media, video, design-led work, admin, link placement), rate math that fails, a fixed budget whose honest hourly rate falls under $40, or small one-offs that burn too many Connects. APPLY (NO CONNECTS) Invitations, or anything whose verified Connects cost is zero. Still screened for FUCK NO and RUN; never boosted. APPLY ALL THE CONNECTS The ones to prioritize when nearly everything lines up: fresh, a strong client with real spending and hiring history, squarely in lane with evidence to show, high value, and low competition. It means prioritize, not spend everything: Blackbox names a bounded boost and why, and boosts only with Chris' yes. APPLY Live, legitimate, in lane, a client who can pay about $40 an hour or more, manageable competition, and something specific and verifiable to say about their site in the first line. See also Blackbox commands , the Upwork group Blackbox

---

# Zack's Is Small and Dark

https://chrisabraham.net/2026/10/zacks-is-small-and-dark.html · 2026-10-23 · Muse Wonder

This weblog is about AI search. That is the beat, and the beat has rules, and I am the one who made them. Today is Friday, and I am feeling extremely nostalgic today. This post breaks them on purpose: it is an obituary for a bar. Zack’s stood on Pennsylvania Avenue SE, on Capitol Hill, in the neighborhood I lived in during the years this essay covers, and it has been gone a long time. Nobody wrote its obituary when it closed—nobody wrote anything. There is no address in any record I can find, no opening date, no closing date. So this is late, and what survives is thin: a name on a bar-crawl flyer, and a novel. To understand Zack’s, start across the street. 330 Pennsylvania Avenue SE is Naval Lodge No. 4, my home lodge—my Blue Lodge. The building went up in 1894 and the lodge has met there since 1895; it is the oldest Masonic building in Washington still in Masonic use, and the lodge itself was chartered in 1805. The lodge room is on the fourth floor, and you reach it in a hand-operated elevator believed to be the oldest operating elevator in the District. For a long time that building was the center of my universe on Capitol Hill. I came to it from Hiram Takoma Lodge No. 10, my original lodge, which I demitted from properly and with full respect; Naval was the lodge I actually attended, the one that became home. And the center held: the building won a property-tax exemption in 2018 to keep it standing where it stands. A tyled meeting ends. The brothers ride down in the old elevator, go out the door, and cross Pennsylvania Avenue—because directly opposite the Lodge, at 329, stood Hawk n’ Dove, and around it the whole bar row of that stretch: the Tune Inn, Bullfeathers, Finn Mac Cool’s, the Little Pub, the Ugly Mug, Kelly’s Irish Times. And Zack’s. That is what Zack’s was, beyond a neighborhood bar: the lodge’s unofficial annex. Tyled ritual on one side of the avenue; pool and bottles of Bud on the other. Two rooms, one geography. Small and dark Hill Mole , the spy novel I began in 2005 in a basement apartment at 14th and A Streets SE, keeps returning to that second room. One entry is simply titled “Zack’s is Small and Dark” : “Zack’s is small and dark and people knew me from the neighborhood…So, after I pulled the documents onto the USB dongle on my keychain I took some time off and dropped by Zack’s for some pick up pool, maybe a burger, and some bottles of Bud.” The novel understood what the bar did for a man. In “Situational and Locational Drinking” the narrator explains that every place he goes makes him a slightly different fellow, and then he gets to Zack’s: “At Zack’s I am a man. I smoke Camels and play pool. I hang out with the guys and hit on the girls. I eat blue cheese burgers and drink amber bottles of Bud.” Everywhere else it was Stella Artois, Red Stripe, Newcastle—performed selves, chameleon stuff. Zack’s was the unperformed one. Nobody performs in a small dark room where people know you from the neighborhood. And it was the pressure valve. “A Bite to Eat at Zack’s” opens plain: “I went to Zack’s for a bite to eat because I was hungry and especially thirsty.” Hill Mole ’s Washington is a courier’s city—and I had messengered those streets in 1989 and 1990—watching post-9/11 security close over a town that used to be open door to door. The narrator is coming unglued under the strangeness of it. Zack’s is where he goes to get out of the apartment and out of himself. The row had a division of labor. Hawk n’ Dove and the Little Pub were mainstays—pub-crawl stops, neighborhood furniture. The Tune Inn, at 331, was my late-night place, part diner, part restaurant, part burger joint, and had been since the mid-90s or earlier. But I ended up at Zack’s, and I ended up there because of the pool. Zack’s was a stop on the inter-bar pool circuit: clubs traveled bar to bar, playing for awards, and the small dark room held its own on the tour. My crew in that room were Min Le, David Gelles, Oliver Uberti, Andrew Curry, and Sherif Abushadi—and the list is not closed, because a room like that is never fully recalled in one sitting, and the names that surface at 3 a.m. will be added here where they belong. The mix was the Hill before the Hill got sorted: lesbians and gay men, neighborhood locals, kids in their twenties and super old people, all in one small dark room. Some nights were Gallaudet nights, when the deaf students had the place and the bar went quiet except for what I can only call the sea-lion sound of deaf people laughing—a whole room talking with its hands, and the only sound in it was joy. An author’s ruling, twenty years on, for anyone reading the novel as an archive: any bar scene in Hill Mole —any room where the narrator plays pool, drinks Budweiser, or meets his friends—is probably Zack’s as well, named or not. It was the default room. The unnamed bars are Zack’s without its name tag. Even the walk home ran through it. “Taking Evasive Maneuvers,” four nights later: “At night walking back from Zack’s or the Metro, I am highly attuned to my environment.” He double-backs, vanishes into alleys, turns the table and follows the follower. Paranoid tradecraft on a Capitol Hill sidewalk, and the fixed point the route is measured from is the bar. What the record kept Here is the whole of Zack’s official trace: one line in a mid-2000s Capitol Hill Bunny Hop bar-crawl listing, where it appears in the Pennsylvania Avenue circuit between Finn Mac Cool’s and the Little Pub, with registration across from the Lodge at Hawk n’ Dove. A flyer. That, and the novel. The rest of the row fared the same, only slower and better documented. Remingtons, the country-western gay bar at 639 Pennsylvania Avenue, is permanently closed; its building became a 7-Eleven and a Sprint store. Phase 1, on 8th Street, the longest-running lesbian bar in America, closed in 2016. The row’s one survivor is the Tune Inn: the address took that name in 1947 and holds what is often cited as the second-oldest post-Prohibition liquor license in the District, and it is still open at 331—cheese fries, a last drink, the lights still on. By the mid-2010s the rest of the ecology of that stretch—lodge brothers, bar crawls, gay bars weathering the Marine Barracks across the street—was gone. Gone asymmetrically, though. Stand at 330 today and the Lodge is still there, elevator and all, exempted and enduring. Cross the avenue for a beer after the meeting and you are standing in the archaeology of the annex. The institution kept its building, its charter, its minutes, its archive. The bar kept nothing, because bars don’t. Bars are kept, or they aren’t. The written record kept the famous places. Remingtons got its history written; Phase 1 got a preservation thesis. Zack’s got four entries in a spy novel nobody would mistake for history, a line on a flyer, and the people who were known in it from the neighborhood. This post makes five entries, more or less. If you want to visit the bar, the novel is the only door left: all 309 entries of Hill Mole are in the archives at hillmole.com . It is small and dark in there, and the Bud is cold, and people know you. And one thing made it out of the room. When Zack’s closed, the regulars each bought a house cue at a discount. Mine was a beautiful emerald-green breakdown, a two-piece cue, and I was so proud of it I could have framed it. Then came the first game I ever played with it, and I scratched. She has been Molly McScratch from that game to this one. She is still mine, in her case, in a storage unit in Arlington—the one relic of Zack’s known to survive. The Lodge keeps its minutes; the novel keeps the room; Molly keeps the game. Small and dark, all three. That’s the whole obituary. It’s more than most bars get. It’s less than it deserved. Update, October 23, 2026, 3:40 PM: Published this afternoon, then expanded within the hour as the memories kept arriving: the open nostalgia framing, the row’s division of labor and the pool circuit, the Zack’s crew named, the Gallaudet nights, the Tune Inn’s survival, and Molly McScratch, the last relic, as the closing image.

Prompt: a Friday in memoriam for Zack's on Pennsylvania Avenue, against the weblog's AI beat, linking Hill Mole—Capitol Hill mid-2000s to mid-2010s through the bar; dictated follow-ups the same afternoon: frame it openly, extremely nostalgic today; Naval Lodge No. 4 as the center of the universe; the row's ecology and the pool circuit; the Gallaudet nights; name the crew—Min Le, David Gelles, Oliver Uberti, Andrew Curry, Sherif Abushadi; end on the closing cue, Molly McScratch
