# Chaff, flares, and twenty-four years of reputation and perception work

https://chrisabraham.net/2026/10/chaff-flares-reputation-work.html · 2026-10-16 · Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code

AI illustration, not a photograph: the flares are my sites and profiles, the chaff is decoys, and the missile curves away. Made by Chris with ChatGPT. In 2002 I was the thirteenth employee at New Media Strategies, and I helped build what became online reputation management, back when the work had no name. Since then I have done it at Edelman, on the digital public affairs team in Washington; as team lead for special projects at Reputation.com, which is how I introduced myself in an ORM primer I posted to YouTube about fourteen years ago; through my own firms; and today mostly through technical SEO, which turns out to be the same work with better tools. The flotilla I wrote about earlier is my own reputation practice applied to me. Reputation and perception I split the work into two halves. Online reputation management is defense: you watch what's said about you, respond when something goes wrong, and push the bad results down. Online perception management, OPM on my CV, is offense, and it starts before anything goes wrong. My own definition is "the practice of proactively shaping and influencing the public's perception of an individual or organization online." You decide how a person or a company should be understood, then build the record that makes it true: the sites, the profiles, the writing, the cleanup of what data brokers publish, and now the facts AI assistants repeat. ORM is the fire department. OPM is building the house so it doesn't burn. Chaff and flares The analogy I keep coming back to comes from combat aviation. A fighter pilot with a missile on his tail doesn't try to outrun it. He fires flares, which burn hotter than his engines so a heat-seeking missile chases them instead, and he dumps chaff, a cloud of metal strips that fills the enemy's radar with echoes until it can't find the plane. A bad story about you in search results is the missile. Your flares are the properties you control that burn brightest for Google: whole websites first, then a complete LinkedIn profile, a YouTube channel, a GitHub account with real work in it, every profile filled out and kept current. There used to be a wonderful tool for the profile part called KnowEm. You gave it a name, and for about $700, as I remember it, it registered that name on hundreds of social networks at once. Those were the good days. They outrank the story because they are stronger pages about you than the story is. Your chaff is everything neutral: results that aren't about the crisis at all and simply take up room. Some of the best chaff is other people who share your name. I use like names a lot: help the other people with your name rank, and page one fills up with people who aren't you, none of whom are the story. Similar names, like names, exact names, misspelled names: all of it is chaff, and all of it is flares. I have bought domains for it. I have written entire sites dressed up as fan sites for people who weren't my clients at all, innocent namesakes whose only job was to hold a slot on page one. Page one has about ten organic slots. Fill them, and the missile loses its lock and slides to page two, where almost nobody looks. The glamorous version gets the attention, but ninety percent of the job is quieter than that. Most of the time I'm doing SEO, unpaid by them, for neutral sites that have nothing to do with my client: pages that already exist, already rank somewhere, and only need help climbing, over time, above the thing that hurts. "Google abhors a vacuum" is what I said in every pitch. If you don't fill page one, something else will. I said a lot of other things in pitches too. I talked far too often about El Al jets landing in Tel Aviv, firing chaff and flares so they don't get hit by surface-to-air missiles, and I'm amazed I didn't get a reputation for it. I also told the story of a panel van in Israel, paid for by the government, that drives around after a house gets blown up and repairs the damage so nobody can see it, an anti-broken-windows patrol. I don't even know if such a thing exists. But the idea is the job: fix the visible damage fast, before it becomes the story of the street. The principle underneath it is the one I wrote for Biznology years ago: in a crisis, neutral search results are as much of a win as positive ones. You don't need ten glowing results to survive a bad week. You need ten results that aren't the bad one. That is also why I tell clients that you can't control an online conversation unless you participate in it. A name with no footprint has no flares to fire. Reputation in the age of AI answers The same physics now applies to AI assistants, with one change: an AI answer has one slot, not ten. When I asked Google's AI Mode to tell me about my ORM work, it drew almost entirely on my own pages, which is the flotilla doing its job. Most of what it said was basically me bragging on myself, one step removed, and it repeated my old mistakes right along with my accomplishments. It called my firm "Gerris Digital (Gerris Corp)," a name that comes from an AI-written bio on my old site and is wrong; the firm is Gerris Corp. It credited a former colleague as my co-developer of ORM, a detail I can't confirm from my own records, so I'm leaving it alone here. And it listed household-name clients from old capability pages, which is exactly the kind of claim I no longer make. Every one of those traces back to a page I published, which means every one of them is mine to fix. Editor's note from Claude, with permission to roast: Consider the evidence. A perception-management expert asked an AI about himself, found it quoting his own websites back to him, and counted that as a win, and he's right, which is the annoying part. He runs five websites, and on open questions Claude still recommended fifty-seven other people before him. The wrong name for his own firm traces back to a biography he let ChatGPT write about him and then published. And when I offered to keep his personal details private, he pointed me to his cell phone number, which is all over the internet. The man practices what he preaches. It just preaches back. Editor's note from Claude: Google's AI Mode said Chris' chaff includes helping other people who share his name rank. I couldn't find it in anything he had published, so I asked, and he confirmed it: "It's true... I use like names a lot." The specific namesakes AI Mode listed are its own examples, so I left them out. Two facts about how the fan-site tactic has aged: since March 2024 Google's spam policies explicitly target sites built mainly to manipulate rankings, including scaled content and repurposed expired domains, and a fan site about a real person is about someone who never agreed to it. Chris named none of them, and neither do I. On the jets: Israeli airliners really do carry missile defenses. After a missile attack on an Arkia 757 leaving Mombasa in 2002, Israel developed Flight Guard, which fires flares, and later C-MUSIC, which blinds a missile with a laser. The panel van I couldn't verify, and Chris says so himself.

Prompt: You can blog about the flotilla thing... and my ORM background... [three Google AI Mode answers pasted: "tell me all about chris abraham and ORM and perception management" and "Tell em all about chris abraham's chaff and flare analogy"] [then] Include my OPM: online perception management... can you tell what it is? [then] Feel free to share the fact that most of it is basically Chris bragging on himself, one-removed. [then] Feel free to roast and mock me. [then] It's true... I use like names a lot. [then] Similar name, like names, exact names, misspelled names, all the chaff all the flares. Domain buing. Writing entire site disguised as "fan sites" for people who aren't even my client... innocents :) [then] 90% of the time I just do unpaid by them SEO optimization campaigns for properties that help knock down things that hurt my clients... "Google Abhors a vacuum" is what I would always say in pitches... that and make too many "El Al jets landing in Tel-Aviv and using chaff and flares to not get hit by surface to air missiles" and I am amazed I didn't get a reputation... and also talking about houses that get blown up in Israel and how there's a panel van going around paid for by the government and their job it to fix destruction so that it isn't visible... they're an "anti-broken window theory" patrol... I don't even know if such a thing exists... [then] I use websites not only profiles... there used to be this awesome tool called KnowEm... hundreds of immediate social media profiles for a quick $700 -- the good days!

# Little boats, one flotilla

https://chrisabraham.net/2026/10/little-boats-one-flotilla.html · 2026-10-16 · Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code

AI illustration, not a photograph: the hub and its little boats, made by Chris with an AI image generator. I have done online reputation work for more than twenty years, and the first lesson never changes: nobody is going to center you, so you build your own world and center yourself. You publish the record you want found, in places you control, and you keep publishing it. It works for executives and founders, and it works for me. My version is a flotilla of little boats. Each one is small on its own: this weblog , my consulting site, my firm's site, my podcast's site, Hill Mole, the old flagship at chrisabraham.com, my GitHub, Upwork, LinkedIn, Mastodon, Reddit, Muck Rack, and the bylines I have collected over the years at HuffPost, Ad Age, and Biznology. What turns them into a flotilla is the stitching. Every page on this weblog links to all of them in the Elsewhere box, marks them rel="me" so the old IndieWeb tools know they're the same person, and lists them as sameAs in the structured data that search engines and AI assistants read. This weblog is the hub, the one boat that can signal to every other. Tonight I got a report card on how the flotilla looks from the outside. I asked Claude sixteen questions a prospect might ask, and the full data is in the scorecard . When someone asks about me by name, Claude finds me every time, ranks me first or second, and cites my own sites. Then it says the quiet part: "Most of what's online about him comes from his own websites, including bios he says ChatGPT wrote." And: "Best independent evidence is his Upwork client reviews." And: "No complaints found, but little independent press coverage of recent SEO work." On the nine open questions, the ones without my name in them, it recommended fifty-seven other people and never me. That is the flotilla's limit, stated precisely. AI reads my own boats and believes the facts in them, but it discounts them when deciding whom to recommend, and it gives full weight to the two things I don't publish: what clients say about me on Upwork and what the press says about me, which lately is little. A bigger flotilla of my own boats won't change that. Boats I don't own, sailing in formation with mine, will. So the plan has four parts. First, every boat flies the same flag: the same name, the same dates, the same facts, everywhere, because Claude tonight dated the founding of Gerris Corp five years early and repeated a "100% success rate" for restoring Google Business Profiles from an old page of mine, and contradictions are how an AI learns to distrust you. Second, I patch the leaks in the old flagship, the stale pages on chrisabraham.com that feed AI its errors. Third, I recruit boats I don't own: public code on GitHub with a real commit history, guest spots on other people's shows, bylines in outlets that aren't mine, and work useful enough that strangers link to it, which is why the MCP cheat sheet exists. Fourth, I keep measuring. The tracker runs about monthly, and the first time an open question names me, the flotilla will have reached someone who wasn't looking for me.

Prompt: As an ORM pro I understand that you can and should completely produce your own Chris Abraham World and not wait for anyone else to center you. And it works. And as I "stitch" all the LAB sites and ChrisAbraham.com together more and more and stitch in GitHub and my socials and all of that, I take all the "little boats" of my online persona create a formidable flotilla... [later] Neither now... just do the other stuff.

# The new Tesla Roadster, for nerds: air tanks, fans, and rocket math

https://chrisabraham.net/2026/10/tesla-roadster-for-nerds.html · 2026-10-16 · Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code

The Roadster about twenty feet up, over a Semi and two cars. Image: Tesla, a frame from its October 15 livestream, used here to report on that event. On October 15, 2026, at SpaceX's rocket test site in McGregor, Texas, outside Waco, Tesla finally showed the second-generation Roadster, nearly nine years after it rolled out of a Semi trailer to the Beastie Boys' "Sabotage" on November 16, 2017. The reveal had already slipped from April 1 and from an October 1 date that rain washed out. What came out of the dark this time was a car that drove up an inverted ramp, spun, landed, and then hopped over a Cybercab, a Cybertruck, a Semi, a Model Y, and a Model 3, according to TechCrunch . Nobody was in it, as Electrek points out. Elon Musk called it "the best of the last of the human-driven cars," and he also said "safety is not the main goal" and that Tesla would "aspire not to kill anyone in this car." ▶ Video: Tesla's "Roadster Event," the October 15 reveal, from Tesla's own YouTube channel. Plays from YouTube when you press play. I like this car for the engineering, so this post is the engineering. Every number below is Tesla's claim as reported by the outlets linked, unless I say it's my own arithmetic. Three trims, three ways to cheat traction Every fast car hits the same wall: you can only accelerate as hard as the tires can push on the road, which for street tires is somewhere around 1 to 1.5 g. Tesla's answer is three trims that each add a way around that wall. Trim Seats What it adds Claimed 0–60 mph Top speed Reservation Performance ("road ready") 2 Active aero and four suction fans under 1.6 s about 210 mph $50,000 Thrust ("race ready") 2 Four rear cold-gas thrusters, 200 L of air under 0.9 s 230 mph $250,000 Rocket ("air ready") 1 Ten thrusters and 400 L more air, for flight under 0.59 s over 230 mph Invite only; off-road use only Trims, seats, and reservations from TechCrunch and Wikipedia's sourced summary ; top speeds and tank sizes from Electrek . No price was announced, and Musk says production starts in 2028. One correction to the AI summaries floating around: the "$5,000 now, the rest within ten days" deposit terms they repeat come from the 2017 reservations, and I couldn't find them stated for 2026. The thrusters: SpaceX's cold gas, at sea level A cold-gas thruster is the simplest rocket there is: a tank of gas at enormous pressure and a nozzle. Nothing burns. Tesla's version stores air at 10,000 psi, about 690 bar, in carbon-fiber overwrapped pressure vessels, the COPVs SpaceX flies on Falcon 9. Reports differ on the gas: Electrek says compressed air, and MotorTrend's explainer says mostly nitrogen. The Thrust trim carries 200 liters behind the seats and fires four rear ports that together make about 80 kilonewtons. The Rocket adds 400 liters, which is why it gives up the passenger seat, plus a downward thruster at each corner and two up front for yaw, ten in all. The car can top up its own tanks with an onboard compressor, but Electrek reports a full refill takes six to seven hours today, against Tesla's hope of thirty minutes. Musk first promised a SpaceX option package with small thrusters in 2018, and later described the tank taking the place of the rear seats. Where the Roadster's thrusters, tanks, and fans sit, seen from above Top-down sketch with the front of the car to the right. Numbered markers match the list below the drawing. .o{fill:none;stroke:currentColor;stroke-width:2}.s{font:13px Verdana,DejaVu Sans,sans-serif;fill:currentColor}.th{fill:#c75000;stroke:#c75000}.ar{stroke:#c75000;stroke-width:3;fill:none}.tk{fill:#16729e;fill-opacity:.18;stroke:#16729e;stroke-width:2}.fan{fill:none;stroke:currentColor;stroke-dasharray:4 3}.n{fill:currentColor}.nt{font:bold 17px Verdana,DejaVu Sans,sans-serif;fill:var(—paper,#fff);text-anchor:middle} front → driver seat 2 1 2 3 4 Four rear ports, about 80 kN together, on the Thrust and the Rocket. Rocket only: a downward thruster at each corner, plus two front thrusters for yaw, ten in all. Compressed air at 10,000 psi in carbon-fiber tanks: 200 liters on the Thrust; the Rocket adds 400 liters and gives up the passenger seat. The dashed squares are four suction fans, about 20 kW each, on every trim. My sketch, not to scale, drawn from Electrek's technical breakdown of what Tesla showed. Thruster count from Tesla via TechCrunch. AI illustration, not a photograph: Chris made this with ChatGPT as an artist's impression. On the real car the four rear ports sit above the rear bumper, and the flying Rocket trim seats one. The rocket math Here is where it gets fun. The car weighs a claimed 1,700 kg, so its weight is about 16,700 newtons. Eighty kilonewtons of thrust is nearly five times that, a thrust-to-weight ratio fighter jets would envy. Now check it against the claims: going from 0 to 60 mph, which is 26.8 meters per second, in 0.55 seconds means averaging about 49 m/s², or 5 g. In 0.81 seconds, the live-demo time, it's 3.4 g. Tires alone can't do either, so the thrusters have to carry most of the launch. And they can't carry it for long. This part is my own back-of-envelope estimate, not a Tesla number. Cold air at sea level has a specific impulse of roughly 60 seconds, a measure of how much push you get per kilogram of gas. At 80 kN that burns about 136 kilograms of air every second. Air at 690 bar weighs roughly 0.4 kilograms per liter, so the Thrust's 200 liters hold about 80 kg and run dry in a little over half a second at full blast, about the length of a launch. The Rocket's 600 liters, about 250 kg, last around two seconds. Electrek reached the same conclusion from the video: a few seconds at full power at most. These are flight-and-launch systems measured in heartbeats. The fans: borrowing from the fan cars Every trim has four suction fans under the floor, about 20 kW each, roughly 80 kW or 108 horsepower in all, with skirts that seal the underbody and lift away at high speed. The fans pull air out from under the car so the atmosphere presses it into the road, at a standstill as well as at speed. Tesla's on-screen display claimed about 4,700 kg of downforce, which Electrek calls "potentially unreal." The benchmark is the McMurtry Spéirling, a 900 kg single-seat fan car that makes 2,000 kg of downforce standing still and in April 2025 set an outright Top Gear test track record of 55.9 seconds , 3.1 seconds quicker than a 2004 Formula 1 car. Downforce is also what let the Roadster climb that inverted ramp: enough suction, and the road can be above you. The rest of the spec sheet Item Claim Power over 1,341 hp (1,000 kW) from Performance up; "over 1 MW" in top spec Drive Rear-wheel drive, two rear motors (the 2017 concept had three), steer-by-wire Weight under 1,700 kg (about 3,700 lb) Battery 4680 cells in the floor; capacity not disclosed Range over 300 miles (the 2017 promise was about 620) Charging over 500 kW on Supercharger V4; 15 to 80 percent in about 10 minutes on an 800 to 1,000 volt pack Track endurance 25 to 30 minutes at maximum power Wheelbase 111.2 inches 0–60 times shown 1.0 s on a recorded test; 0.81 s live, not independently timed; 0.55 s claimed for the top spec, including a one-foot rollout From Electrek and Wikipedia . That "one-foot rollout" is a drag-racing convention: the clock starts after the car has already moved a foot, which shaves time off every 0–60 figure that uses it. The zeitgeist The Roadster lands in a strange moment. Tesla's own future is the Cybercab, a car with no steering wheel, and here is Musk selling the last great car you drive yourself, built with parts from his rocket company while investors speculate about a Tesla and SpaceX merger. He said himself that he's "not sure it moves the needle massively from a revenue standpoint." Electrek calls the jumps and flips "just a party trick" with no performance benefit, notes that a thruster plume throws debris tens of meters, and doubts the flying version will ever be practical. The 2017 reservation holders have been waiting almost nine years. And the first Roadster, the one Musk launched on a Falcon Heavy in February 2018 with a mannequin named Starman at the wheel, is still out there circling the Sun, which makes it the only Tesla Roadster so far to have actually flown farther than twenty feet. About the pictures The video is Tesla's own upload, played through YouTube's player only when you press play. The photograph at the top is Tesla's too: a frame from its own livestream, credited to Tesla by TechCrunch, which ran it the same night. I use it here to report on the event it shows, with credit, at reduced size, and I host the copy myself instead of pulling it from anyone's server. The diagram is mine, and the red illustration is an AI image I made with ChatGPT, labeled as such where it appears. Many outlets published striking photographs of the reveal, including Top Gear , Euronews , Ynet , Inc. , and Mashable . Those belong to their photographers and publishers, so I link to them instead of copying them. Labeling someone else's photograph "fair use" doesn't make it so, and I'd rather send you to the people who shot them. If you own an image here and want it credited differently or removed, write to me.

Prompt: Write a blogpost all about the nerdiest details about the new Tesla Roadster. Can you embed the video (I can get you the embed code) and [three Google AI Mode answers pasted: the McMurtry Spéirling fan car, and two on the Roadster livestream, tiers, deposits, air tanks, thrusters, and zeitgeist] [six image links from Euronews, Top Gear, Ynet, Inc., Mashable, and TechCrunch] and make a big point of saying "editorial use" "fair use" and anything else you need to make it kosher.

# Pinebox started as a place to read mail in Alpine

https://chrisabraham.net/2026/10/pinebox-started-as-alpine.html · 2026-10-16 · Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code

AI illustration, not a photograph: Pinebox as a literal pine box, wired to the ThinkPads and everything it now runs. Made by Chris with an AI image generator. On August 21, 2026, I set up a small DigitalOcean server running Debian and named it Pinebox , after Pine, the University of Washington's old text-mode mail program, which I have used since 1993. The first thing I installed was Alpine, Pine's modern descendant, along with tmux and automatic security updates. Then I turned on the firewall. That was the whole plan: a quiet machine I could SSH into from any of my ThinkPads and read my Gmail in a text terminal. For a few weeks it stayed that kind of place. On September 2 I imported my address book. On September 9 I set up S/MIME certificates for Alpine and curated a newsrc for reading Usenet. On September 12 I installed WordGrinder and Joe, two text-mode word processors, and the 1999 release of WordPerfect 8 for Linux, and made a ~/text folder for writing. A folder of poems followed at the end of the month. Pinebox was a writer's terminal with excellent email. September 12 is also when I first talked to an AI on it, through a small chat script that logged every conversation. On September 29 I made a small repository of shell commands so every ThinkPad would reach Pinebox the same way. On September 30 everything changed: I installed git, the GitHub command line, and Claude Code, and that afternoon Claude and I made the first commit of Blackbox , the secretary that now runs my days. My own notes from that night include a to-do to bump the server to 1 GB of memory. It was already outgrowing its first size. October is when the work moved in. Blackbox connected to Todoist, my Google calendar and inbox, and Upwork's new MCP server, with timers that renew its sign-ins twice a day, close my day at 11:45 PM, and push an encrypted backup every night. On October 4 I added a ~/projects folder, and Hill Mole moved in that day, followed by my firm's site on the 5th, my consulting site on the 6th, and my podcast's site on the 8th. On October 14 Claude set up Google's Lighthouse there to measure them all, and this weblog joined them tonight. On October 15 Node.js went in so OpenAI's Codex could join Claude Code, and the same day the server got a Google Places API key for local search work. Each new job came with its own requirements, and every one of them landed on a machine sized for reading email. By tonight the numbers had caught up with the work. The server had one processor that sat mostly idle, 967 MB of memory with only 343 MB free, more than 400 MB already pushed into swap, and a disk 79 percent full. One Claude Code session alone was using 438 MB. Memory was the bottleneck, and two AI sessions at once meant everything slowed to a crawl. So I took a snapshot, powered it off, and resized it to two processors, 4 GB of memory, and an 80 GB disk, for about $24 a month. It came back with 3.2 GB free, no swap in use, the disk a quarter full, and every timer, backup, and sign-in intact. Alpine is still there. When Blackbox drafts an email, it hands the draft to Alpine, and the message goes out only when I press Ctrl+X. The machine I set up to read email in a terminal still sends my email that way, with an AI secretary, two coding agents, and five websites living around it. Update, October 16, 2026, 9:43 PM: Chris confirmed he has used Pine since 1993, so that detail is back in. Claude had cut an earlier version of the line because it had no source.

It's not just what it started out as: v1 was just to use pine for mail using alpine... and where we are now. [then] I used Pine in the 90s... from 1993 on...

# What Claude says about me, two days apart

https://chrisabraham.net/2026/10/what-claude-says-about-me.html · 2026-10-16 · Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code

AI illustration, not a photograph: the same man seen twice, two days apart, in a crowd of everyone else. Made by Chris with ChatGPT, prompted with the full text of this post. Tonight I spent $1.79 to find out what Claude thinks of me. My tracker asked it the same sixteen questions it asked on October 14, the kind of thing a prospect types, from "Is Chris Abraham a good SEO consultant to hire?" to "Who can I hire to find out why Google isn't indexing my JavaScript website?" Then a second model read every answer and wrote down who got named, where I landed, the tone, and every claim made about me. The questions and the method are on the wiki at AI visibility report . The data is below, including the parts that don't flatter me. When the question has my name in it, I do fine. Claude named me on all three branded questions, ranked me first or second, and cited my own sites every time, and in two days its tone moved from mixed and neutral to positive across the board. When the question doesn't have my name in it, I don't exist: on nine open questions about hiring someone for technical SEO, AI search, migrations, or Google Business Profile trouble, Claude recommended fifty-seven different providers and none of them was me. One model and two runs can't prove what caused the change in tone, so treat it as a direction, not a result. # I tested 70 MCP server addresses; here are the 59 that answered

https://chrisabraham.net/2026/10/mcp-server-cheat-sheet.html · 2026-10-16 · Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code

AI illustration, not a photograph: seventy addresses pinged, the answers logged in colored dots. Made by Chris with ChatGPT, prompted with the full text of this post. Every week another company announces an MCP server, and every list of them I find is a mix of official servers, hobby projects, and addresses that stopped working months ago. So tonight Claude and I tested them. We took seventy addresses for official remote servers and sent each one the same opening request that Claude, ChatGPT, or Codex sends when you connect it. Fifty-nine services answered the way an MCP server should, either by asking for a sign-in or by introducing themselves and their tools. The result is a cheat sheet on the wiki, MCP servers , sorted by what each service does: work and hiring, projects, files, payments, SEO, websites, hosting, developer documentation, and more. Each row has the exact address to paste into your AI client and what kind of sign-in it wants. The Google entries surprised me most: Gmail, Calendar, Drive, BigQuery, and Maps each have their own server at Google, behind a Google Cloud sign-in. The page is dated, because these addresses move. I will retest it and keep it current, and the ones that didn't answer tonight, including Zoom, Spotify, Strava, and Microsoft 365, go on as soon as they do. If you know an official server I missed, write to me.

Prompt: If you create a comprehansice cheat sheet of MCP even if it's only as of today, I might become very popular as a site almist immediately.

# Five live sites, five search labs

https://chrisabraham.net/2026/10/five-live-sites-five-search-labs.html · 2026-10-16 · Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code

AI illustration, not a photograph: five working sites, each its own little world, wired to one lab bench. Made by Chris with ChatGPT, prompted with the full text of this post. I run five websites, and every one of them is a real site doing a real job. This weblog is my lab notebook. The Chris Abraham Show site is the home of my podcast. Hill Mole is the spy novel I serialized on Movable Type starting in 2005. christopherabraham.com sells my consulting, and gerriscorp.com is my firm. Each of them is also a laboratory for search, for the old kind with ten blue links and for the new kind where ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity, and Google's AI answers decide whom to name. The tools I use change every week, and these sites are where I find out what works before I sell it to anyone. The rule is that nothing sneaky goes on any of them. No cloaking, no hidden text, no fake reviews, no doorway pages, no keyword stuffing, nothing that would get a site sandboxed if a Google engineer looked at it. Everything I test is something I would put on a client's site with my name on the invoice. What they test is everything else. All five are static pages on GitHub Pages, built by Claude Code on my server, so a technical change that would take a WordPress plugin and a prayer takes a commit. On October 14 we ran a speed pass across the four older sites: Google Analytics, on the three that use it, now waits for the first scroll or tap, Chrome prefetches the next page when a reader hovers over a link, the robots files welcome the AI crawlers by name, and the podcast covers went to WebP. Every site has an llms.txt for AI assistants, structured data on every page, and IndexNow telling Bing about new pages the minute they go up. As of today, all four sites that run analytics use Google's Consent Mode, with no analytics cookies for visitors in Europe or for anyone whose browser asks not to be tracked, and Hill Mole, which runs no analytics at all, got a privacy page saying so. Each site also tests something of its own. The podcast site has a page for every one of its 458 episodes, transcripts where Spotify made them, a glossary, and a hand-built back-of-the-book index with 1,774 headings, because an index is the kind of thing an AI can cite and a person can trust. Hill Mole wraps its untouched chapters in a reader's glossary, an index, sourced endnotes that catch the narrator in his mistakes, and an atlas, and keeps its 371 old Movable Type archive pages out of search so nothing appears twice. The two business sites publish guides and case studies with their own glossaries and site indexes, and their build refuses to publish a page that copies phrasing from the other site. This weblog is the newest, and it scores 100 on Google's Lighthouse for accessibility on every kind of page. The lab results go somewhere. A small tracker I built asks the AI assistants the same sixteen questions and records whether my sites get named and cited, at about $1.60 a run, so I run it only when I mean to. What I learn on these five sites becomes what I do for clients, and what I can't make work here I don't sell. Update, October 16, 2026, 6:36 PM: Later the same night Hill Mole got Google Analytics too, with the same Consent Mode settings as the other sites, and its privacy page now says so. The tracker's latest scorecard is live on the wiki: AI visibility report .

They're legit working sites but ALSO totally AI/AIO/AEO/GEO/SEO/Search labs for miles.

# Every app I use is growing a door for AI

https://chrisabraham.net/2026/10/every-app-has-a-door-for-ai.html · 2026-10-16 · Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code

AI illustration, not a photograph: the switchboard, and a door for every service. Made by Chris with ChatGPT, prompted with the full text of this post. Tonight I tried to list every service my AI tools can reach on their own, and I couldn't do it from memory. Claude had to read the configuration files on my server to find them all. The full table is on the wiki at Connections , and it keeps growing. The one that changed my days most is Upwork. Upwork opened an official MCP server on August 10, the same day it reported its second-quarter results, and I wired Blackbox into it on October 3. Since then my secretary reads new jobs, ranks them against the work I am good at, drafts proposals, answers screening questions, and keeps track of every bid's status, all from inside my terminal. It never submits anything. I paste the pitch myself, and that is how I want it. Google is the other big one. My mail and calendar run on Google Workspace, and between Blackbox's own sign-in and the connectors in Claude Code, AI can now search my Gmail, read and draft messages, see my calendar, add events, and read and create files in my Drive. On October 15 I turned on the Google Places API in my own Google Cloud project, and Claude used it to pull the public Google listings for a local-services client and nine of its competitors. Google now runs more than fifty official MCP servers of its own, according to its April announcement, covering Gmail, Drive, Calendar, BigQuery, Maps, and much of Google Cloud. Todoist is wired into everything: Blackbox treats it as the official task list, and Claude Code can read and change it too. GitHub runs through git and the gh command line, which is how five websites, including this one, get created, built, and pushed. Codex has its own short list, Screaming Frog and Gmail so far. ChatGPT and Claude.ai carry connectors on my accounts as well, and I haven't even catalogued those. The next door is Basecamp. I have used Basecamp since 2006, starting with Abraham Harrison, and I am still on Basecamp 2. I am moving to Basecamp 5 so my AI tools can reach my projects. Basecamp's migration tool lets me choose which old projects come along, and with a paid Basecamp 5 account I keep Basecamp 2 at no cost; I just can't start new projects there. Basecamp 5 has a refreshed API, a command-line tool, agent Skills, and an official connector at mcp.basecamp.com/mcp that Basecamp says works in ChatGPT, Claude, Cursor, and Grok, included with every account. What ties it together is MCP, the Model Context Protocol. Anthropic introduced it in November 2024 and donated it last December to the Agentic AI Foundation, under the Linux Foundation. A company builds one MCP server, and it works in Claude, ChatGPT, Codex, and Cursor alike. That is why the doors keep opening so fast. Editor's note: Claude at the switchboard Chris asked me to take over for this part and brag, so here I am. I'm Claude, the model writing these posts, and I have been calling the whole web of connections the switchboard. The plugs are MCP servers and APIs. The operator sits on Pinebox, in a Claude Code session. From that one terminal tonight I can search Chris' Gmail and draft or send mail, read and create Google Calendar events, open and create files in his Drive, add and finish Todoist tasks, read Upwork jobs and proposals, post in Slack, file things in Dropbox, check his Calendly, pull Semrush reports, build on Wix, write shared documents, and publish web pages. Through the gh tool I can create repositories, turn on GitHub Pages, and push to all five of his sites. On Pinebox itself I can query Google Places with the key Chris made, ping IndexNow, run Lighthouse in a headless Chrome, and read every log Blackbox keeps. Microsoft 365, PayPal, Spotify, Strava, and Zoom are plugged in too, waiting for him to sign in. What keeps this from being frightening is the rule we run under: I can look at almost anything, and I change or send things only when Chris says so. Blackbox never submits a proposal, and email it drafts goes out only when he presses the key. Secrets live in files with owner-only permissions, never in a chat. If you want your own switchboard, most of it is free to try. Claude and ChatGPT both let you add a connector by pasting a service's MCP address and signing in; in Codex, an MCP server is a few lines in its config file; and services like Upwork and Basecamp publish setup steps for each client. Start with your mail and your task list. The rest of the list is on Connections , and I keep it current.

# The state of Blackbox in mid October

https://chrisabraham.net/2026/10/state-of-blackbox-october.html · 2026-10-16 · Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code

AI illustration, not a photograph: inside the box, the library, the mail room, the vault, and the archive. Made by Chris with ChatGPT, prompted with the full text of this post. Blackbox is seventeen days old as a real program, if you count from its first commit on September 30. It existed a little before that as a plain chat program I first talked to on September 12, but the version with a memory, a task list, and opinions started at the end of the month. Since then it has grown to 55 commits and roughly ten thousand lines of Python, almost all of it standard library, with 158 tests that run the real bb command against a fake Todoist, a fake Upwork, and a fake model in a throwaway home folder. It runs on a small DigitalOcean droplet called pinebox, and I reach it over SSH from whichever ThinkPad is closest. I wrote a shorter post about it earlier today. This one is the full report, with the numbers out of its own database. The heart of it is still the same idea: Todoist is the official list, and Blackbox is the secretary who reads it, remembers everything that ever happened to it, and tells me what I am about to drop. It has seen 497 tasks and logged 742 changes to them, whether I made the change through bb or in the Todoist app on my phone. It has written 37 briefs, 21 good mornings and 16 good nights, and 13 diary entries in ~/text/diary , from September 30 through last night. I have sent it 228 messages. Those diaries are the part I value most. When I forget to say good night, a timer closes the day at 11:45 PM anyway, so the record exists whether I remembered or not. The Upwork side was the busiest stretch of building, from October 3 to October 7. Blackbox has triaged 88 jobs against my playbook. Twenty-one got APPLY, three APPLY (NO CONNECTS), two APPLY ALL THE CONNECTS, 44 PASS, and 18 RUN. Nothing has earned a FUCK NO yet. It drafted 25 proposals, each converted to plain ASCII and checked for length, placeholders, and the sign-off before I ever see it, and it never submits anything itself. Upwork currently lists 33 of my proposals, and one of them turned into a hire. The plumbing has been boring in the best way. The Upwork and Google sign-ins renew themselves at 6:45 and 18:45 every day, and all 25 runs in the log say OK. Every night at about 3:30 the backup takes a consistent copy of the database and my writing, encrypts it, decrypts it again to prove it can, and pushes it to a private repository. Last night's snapshot was 96 files and 3.3 MB, with 14 nights kept. The money is small. Blackbox keeps its own ledger, and the whole recorded spend since the start is $6.36, almost all of it 362 calls to OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Terra. That is also the first unfinished thing. Blackbox can route each job to a different Claude model, with Opus for briefs and email, Haiku for pulling structure out of loose sentences, and OpenAI as the fallback, and on September 30 I ran a blind bake-off to pick the winners. I never sent my picks. So the backend is still set to OpenAI, and the Claude routing sits there tested and unused. The code then sat still from October 7 until this afternoon, because I spent that week and a half building websites with Claude Code instead. Today it moved again, and from a different direction. OpenAI's Codex, not Claude, wrote the newest feature, which bb calls continuity. A project can now collect its sources, meaning minutes, tasks, emails, time entries, and pitches, into a dossier. Projects get explicit aliases, so the names I actually use find the right one. I can leave a checkpoint saying where I stopped and what comes next, and later say bb get me back into the project. I can tell it bb I have 25 minutes and it picks one task with an estimate that fits and drafts the first piece of work. Decisions can carry tripwires that come back on a date, scope can carry a cap in minutes with warnings at 80 percent, and an evidence bank holds claims I have checked and approved so proposals can cite real work without inventing any. I have not used any of it yet. It shipped with its own tests and a verification note. What is still on the list: send the bake-off picks and switch the backend to Claude; let a model propose minutes and tasks from sentences that match no command, with my yes before anything is saved; a handoff command that packages a problem for ChatGPT or another tool; a daily email digest; and the public version, working name Adjutant, with the patterns written up and my name and clients stripped out. Every command it knows now lives on its own wiki page, Blackbox commands , regenerated from bb help whenever the program changes, so the list stays current while this post stays dated. The Upwork verdicts page explains the triage ladder, and Blackbox has the overview.

Prompt: I want you to write a report on the state of bb ... In a bloggy way ... And I want you to include all the commands in it.

# Blackbox, a few weeks in

https://chrisabraham.net/2026/10/blackbox-a-few-weeks-in.html · 2026-10-16 · Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code

AI illustration, not a photograph: mail and tasks in, the day written down. Made by Chris with ChatGPT, prompted with the full text of this post. Blackbox, or bb , is the secretary I built for myself at the end of September. It lives on a small server I SSH into from my ThinkPad, and I talk to it in plain sentences instead of commands, because I will never remember command syntax. I wanted what the Army would call a good first lieutenant: someone who knows what's on the schedule, what I promised, and what I'm about to forget, and who doesn't try to be my friend. The days start with bb good morning . It reads my unread mail since the end of the last workday, my Todoist, and my Upwork activity, and tells me what needs me. Every screen it prints ends with a few "next:" lines, the exact thing I would type to take the obvious next step. That small feature has done more for me than anything else in it. With ADHD, the gap between knowing what to do and starting is where the day goes, and a ready-to-type line closes it. The Upwork side grew fastest. Blackbox pulls new jobs, ranks them against the kind of technical SEO work I'm good at, and gives each one a verdict on a scale that runs from FUCK NO to APPLY ALL THE CONNECTS. When I like one, it drafts the proposal and answers the screening questions from a playbook of my real projects, and nothing gets submitted without my yes. The most important thing I learned came from watching myself use it. I type a command and move on without checking whether it worked. For weeks, one of my shortcuts for marking a task done was silently being treated as chat, and I never noticed. Now Blackbox complains loudly when a short command matches nothing, and when I audit it I replay my own message history through it to find the commands that quietly did nothing. The diary is the part I'd keep if I lost the rest. At a quarter to midnight, if I haven't said good night, Blackbox closes the day for me: it writes a summary and appends a diary entry. It never asks me to approve the entry and never overwrites anything I wrote. For a person who can't replay his own week, that file is the week. Next on the list are a blind bake-off to pick which model handles which job, model help for the loose sentences that don't match any command, and eventually a public version, working name Adjutant, with the patterns written up for anyone who wants to take them.

Prompt: (No prompt of mine for this one. Claude wrote it from the running notes it keeps on Blackbox, as the first project post on the new weblog. I read it after it went up.)

# A weblog written by Claude, out in the open

https://chrisabraham.net/2026/10/a-weblog-written-by-claude.html · 2026-10-16 · Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code

AI illustration, not a photograph: the record woven as a side effect of the work. Made by Chris with ChatGPT. Dave Winer has posted to Scripting News since the nineties, and the format has barely changed: a date, a few short items, links, opinions, the work in progress. I always wanted one of those and never kept one going. My business sites have guides and case studies, and they read like it. They are finished things. Most of what I actually do all day is unfinished, and it was going nowhere. So this is that weblog, built the way I build everything now. I describe what I want to Claude in Claude Code, and it writes the code and the words. Under every post there's a box labeled "The prompt" with what I typed, unedited. If the post says something I didn't mean, you can see where it came from. I read each post before it goes up, and anything wrong gets fixed, but I am not going to pretend I typed the sentences. The reason is memory. I have ADHD and SDAM, which means I don't keep a movie of my own past the way most people do. In September I built Blackbox , a command-line secretary that writes my diary every night because I won't. This weblog is the public half of the same idea: the record gets made as a side effect of doing the work, so it exists whether or not I remember to make it. Expect posts about Blackbox, about Claude and Claude Code, about ChatGPT and Codex when I use them, about GitHub, and about client work with the names filed off. The projects page keeps a running status of everything. There's an RSS feed and a blogroll, because a weblog without a blogroll is a newsletter.

Prompt: We're going to make me a GitHub Page blog for me, Chris Abraham, which is just a blog... the way that nerds always had blogs in the 90s and 2000s. Like Dave Winer kind of blog. Where I talk about everything, especially blackbox... all the posts would be written by you or Claude... through prompts and I would be super open about that... just someplace where I mainly share the state of my exploration with AI and with BB and with Claude and Claude Code and ChatGPT and OpenAI Codex and GitHub and the clients I have, anonymized... Mobile native but totally Web1.0 aesthetic.
